title: The 1918 influenza pandemic

confidence.note: The pandemic's waves are well documented in contemporary mortality records. Two things remain contested: where it began (Kansas, a British army base in France and China have all been proposed, and the evidence cannot settle it) and how many it killed, with serious estimates running from about 17 million to 100 million.

place: Worldwide; first well described in the United States, March 1918
people: John M. Barry, historian who argues for an origin in Haskell County, Kansas
Jeffery Taubenberger, pathologist whose team sequenced the virus from preserved tissue
summary: A new flu virus circled the world in three waves, killing young adults in their prime. Nobody knows where it began, or exactly how many it killed.
body: In the spring of 1918 a new influenza virus began moving through army camps and cities. Within about a year it had swept across Europe, Asia and North America in three distinct waves, the first best described in the United States in March 1918. The second wave, in the autumn of 1918, was far deadlier than the first and accounted for most of the deaths. An estimated 500 million people were infected, roughly a third of the world's population, and more than 2.5% of those who fell ill died, against less than 0.1% in other influenza pandemics.

What made it uniquely frightening was who died. Influenza normally kills the very young and the very old; in 1918 the death curve gained a third peak among adults of about 20 to 40. Many victims died of bacterial pneumonia that followed the viral infection, in an age with no antibiotics and no flu vaccine.

The name "Spanish flu" is an accident of war. Spain was neutral, so its newspapers reported the epidemic freely while the warring nations censored theirs, and the disease seemed to come from there. Its true birthplace is unknown. The historian John Barry argues for Haskell County, Kansas, in January 1918; the virologist John Oxford pointed to a British army base in France in 1916; others suggested China. Two leading researchers concluded that the historical and genetic evidence cannot identify the origin.
The death toll is just as uncertain. The figure most often quoted is about 50 million, and some estimates run to 100 million; a 2018 reanalysis of national mortality data arrived at 17.4 million.

The virus itself was recovered decades later. Fragments of its genetic material survived in preserved tissue from people who died in 1918, and in 2005 researchers announced that they had used them to rebuild the complete virus. Almost all influenza A infections since 1918 have been caused by its descendants.

myth.record: Spain was simply the country whose uncensored wartime press reported it most openly. Where the virus first emerged is unknown; Kansas, France and China have all been proposed.

links.note: In 1918 nobody could yet see or culture the virus responsible.
The pandemic most often compared with 1918.
Antibiotics later tamed the bacterial pneumonias that killed many flu victims.

title: Insulin

confidence.note: Laboratory notebooks, letters and hospital records in Toronto document the work day by day. What is argued over is credit: the Nobel committee honored two of the four Toronto researchers, and earlier extracts made elsewhere, notably Paulescu's in Bucharest, have their champions.

place: University of Toronto and Toronto General Hospital, Canada
people: Frederick Banting (1891–1941), surgeon who proposed the research
Charles Best (1899–1978), recent physiology graduate and Banting's assistant
James Bertram Collip, biochemist who purified the extract
J. J. R. Macleod, professor of physiology who directed the laboratory
Leonard Thompson, the first patient treated
Nicolae Paulescu (1869–1931), Romanian physiologist with a rival claim
summary: In a Toronto winter a starving diabetic boy got a pancreas extract that worked. Four men made it happen, two got the Nobel, and the credit fight never quite ended.
body: Before insulin, a child with what is now called type 1 diabetes faced a slow death that doctors could only delay by near-starvation. When Leonard Thompson was admitted to Toronto General Hospital in December 1921 he weighed only 65 pounds and was being fed 450 calories a day.

The idea behind his rescue came from Frederick Banting, a surgeon and part-time demonstrator in London, Ontario, who persuaded J. J. R. Macleod, a leading expert on carbohydrate metabolism at the University of Toronto, to give him space, dogs and an assistant, Charles Best, a recent physiology graduate. In December 1921 James Collip, a biochemist on sabbatical from the University of Alberta, joined them to help purify the extracts they were making from the pancreas.

On 11 January 1922 Thompson received Banting and Best's extract. Nothing improved, and an abscess formed where it went in. Collip, in a burst of work between 12 December and 19 January, found how to trap the hormone in a purer form using alcohol, and on 23 January his extract brought Thompson's blood sugar down dramatically. Production was soon handed to the Connaught Laboratories and Eli Lilly, and the patent was sold to the University of Toronto for a token $1.

The 1923 Nobel Prize went to Banting and Macleod. Banting, furious at sharing it with Macleod, announced that he would split his money with Best; Macleod then split his with Collip. Historians, following Michael Bliss's 1982 account, now credit all four.

Toronto was not alone. Macleod reckoned there had been about 400 earlier attempts at a pancreatic treatment, and Nicolae Paulescu in Bucharest had published results with a pancreatic extract he called pancreina in 1921. Toronto's achievement was an extract safe and reliable enough to keep people alive. Paulescu's claim has been complicated by his role in founding far-right, antisemitic political organizations; a tribute to his scientific work planned for Paris in 2003 was cancelled after the Simon Wiesenthal Center accused him of antisemitism.

myth.record: It was a four-person effort: Collip's purification turned the extract into a usable drug and Macleod directed the work. Several researchers abroad, including Paulescu, had earlier made extracts that lowered blood sugar in animals.

links.note: Insulin was one of the first hormones to be turned into a treatment.
A century later, another gut and pancreas hormone became a blockbuster drug.

title: BCG vaccine

confidence.note: The first vaccination in July 1921 and the 1930 Lübeck disaster are both well documented; a detailed official investigation of Lübeck was published at the time.

people: Albert Calmette, bacteriologist at the Pasteur Institute
Camille Guérin, his collaborator
summary: Two Pasteur Institute scientists tamed a cattle germ over 13 years to make a tuberculosis vaccine. A deadly mix-up in Lübeck nearly sank it.
body: At the Pasteur Institute, Albert Calmette and Camille Guérin spent 13 years passing a strain of *Mycobacterium bovis*, the agent of cattle tuberculosis, through more than 200 subcultures containing bile until it no longer caused disease. In July 1921 the first newborn was vaccinated: a baby whose mother had died of tuberculosis and who faced being raised by an infected grandmother. In 1930 in Lübeck, 251 babies were given vaccine accidentally contaminated with virulent human tuberculosis bacilli cultured in the vaccine laboratory; 72 died of it. Investigators showed the fault was the contamination, not BCG.

links.note: Koch had identified the tuberculosis bacillus in 1882.
Weakening a germ in the laboratory was Pasteur's method.

title: Berger records the brain's rhythms

confidence.note: Berger's 1929 paper fixes the publication date, and a modern biographical account gives 6 July 1924 for his first recorded current, so the 1924 date rests on later retelling of his lab records. Electrical activity had been recorded from animal brains since Caton in 1875.

people: Hans Berger (1873–1941), psychiatrist at the University of Jena
Richard Caton, Liverpool physiologist who recorded animal brain currents in 1875
summary: A Jena psychiatrist chasing the physics of telepathy picked up faint electrical waves from the human head, then worked in near-isolation for five years before publishing.
body: Hans Berger, a psychiatrist in Jena who had long hoped to find a physical basis for what he called telepathy, detected a feeble current from electrodes around a scar on a patient's scalp on 6 July 1924. Working alone in the evenings, he refined the method for five years before publishing in 1929. He described the alpha rhythm and its blocking when the eyes open. Animal brain currents had been recorded since Richard Caton in 1875, but Berger's human traces gained little acknowledgment until 1934, when Edgar Adrian and Brian Matthews, who had set out to show they were artifacts, reproduced them.

links.note: The same string-galvanometer technology had already recorded the heart.

sources.title: An appraisal to Hans Berger by the time of his 150th birthday: the human EEG and tales of blood flow, heat and brain waves
sources.supports: Telepathy motive; first current on 6 July 1924 around a scalp scar; evening work and 1929 publication; alpha rhythm and blocking; Adrian and Matthews's confirmation.
sources.quote: Berger worked in the evening between 5:00 and 8:00 p.m. in almost complete isolation and perfected his method for five years before publishing his first report on human EEG in 1929

title: Eugenics and forced sterilization

confidence.note: The laws, the Supreme Court opinion and the Nazi programs are documented in official records. National totals of sterilizations and killings are reconstructions from incomplete records, so figures are rounded.

people: Francis Galton, English scientist and Darwin's cousin, credited with the word eugenics
Carrie Buck, the first person sterilized under Virginia's law
Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr., Supreme Court justice who wrote the Buck v. Bell opinion
summary: Mainstream science once held that the 'unfit' should be stopped from having children. Courts agreed, states sterilized, and Nazi Germany went on to murder.
body: The word "eugenics" is credited to Francis Galton, Darwin's cousin, and by the early twentieth century the movement had spread across Europe and North America as respectable science. Indiana passed the first compulsory sterilization law in 1907; by 1937 thirty-two American states had them. In *Buck v. Bell*, decided on 2 May 1927, the US Supreme Court upheld Virginia's law by eight votes to one, Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes writing that "three generations of imbeciles are enough." Carrie Buck was sterilized. The historian Paul Lombardo later found she had done adequately at school and had become pregnant after being raped by her foster mother's nephew.

Germany's sterilization law of 14 July 1933 was followed by the sterilization of some 400,000 people before the Second World War. From 1939 the regime moved to killing: under Aktion T4, almost 70,000 disabled people had been murdered by the time the program was officially halted in August 1941, and the killing continued unofficially until the end of the war. Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden also passed sterilization laws in the 1930s; compensation has since been paid to victims.

myth.tradition: Carrie Buck was feeble-minded, the daughter of a feeble-minded mother and the mother of a feeble-minded child, as the Supreme Court said.
myth.record: Her school records were adequate, her daughter later made the honor roll, and her pregnancy resulted from rape. The case was built to test the law, not to establish facts about her.

links.note: Eugenicists claimed the authority of the new science of heredity.
Another state-backed abuse of people deemed expendable.
The Nazi doctors' trial, which grew out of the regime's medical crimes, produced the Code.

title: Penicillin

confidence.note: Fleming's 1929 paper, the Oxford team's Lancet papers of 1940–41 and wartime production records document the story well. The dispute is over credit, which popular accounts long gave almost entirely to Fleming.

place: St Mary's Hospital, London; Oxford; Peoria, Illinois
people: Alexander Fleming (1881–1955), bacteriologist at St Mary's Hospital
Howard Florey, who led the Oxford team
Ernst Chain, biochemist who purified penicillin
Norman Heatley, who worked out how to grow the mold in quantity
Andrew Jackson Moyer, US Department of Agriculture scientist in Peoria
summary: A stray mold on a London culture plate took twelve years, an Oxford team and an Illinois corn by-product to become the drug that changed medicine.
body: In 1928 Alexander Fleming, a bacteriologist at St Mary's Hospital in London, noticed that a mold contaminating one of his staphylococcus plates had cleared a zone around itself where bacteria would not grow. He identified it as a *Penicillium*, named its active substance penicillin and published in 1929. But he could not purify the unstable compound, and for a decade almost nothing happened.

In 1939 Howard Florey assembled a team at Oxford. Ernst Chain purified penicillin, and Norman Heatley found ways to grow the mold in bulk. In their key experiment, eight mice were infected with streptococci and four were given penicillin; by morning the untreated mice were dead and the treated ones alive. The results appeared in *The Lancet* in August 1940. In February 1941 an Oxford policeman with abscesses all over his body became the first patient; he improved startlingly, but the supply ran out and he died weeks later.

Wartime Britain could not manufacture the drug, so in June 1941 Florey and Heatley took the mold to the US Department of Agriculture laboratory in Peoria, Illinois. There Andrew Moyer suggested growing it in corn steep liquor, a cheap waste product of cornstarch making, and a strain from a moldy cantaloupe proved six times more productive than Fleming's. At the end of 1942 there was enough penicillin for fewer than 100 patients; by September 1943, enough for the Allied armed forces.

Fleming became the public face of the drug after treating a dying patient in 1942 with Oxford-made penicillin and talking freely to the press, while Florey forbade his team to give interviews. The 1945 Nobel Prize went jointly to Fleming, Chain and Florey. Fleming was also not the first to report that molds can act against bacteria: in 1895 the Italian naval physician Vincenzo Tiberio had published on the antibacterial effects of mold extracts.

myth.tradition: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin and gave the world its first antibiotic.
myth.record: Fleming observed the effect and named the substance, but turning it into a medicine was the work of the Oxford team under Florey and of American government and industrial laboratories. Fleming's outsized fame owed much to wartime publicity.

links.note: Ehrlich's 'magic bullet' was the dream penicillin finally realized for bacterial infections.
The sulfa drugs reached patients first and revived interest in antibacterial chemotherapy.
Penicillin's success launched the hunt for more antibiotics.
Bacteria began evolving resistance almost as soon as antibiotics were used.

title: The iron lung

confidence.note: The machine's design and first clinical use were published in 1929. It was not the first body-enclosing respirator: Drinker's patents were overturned because such devices went back to 1864.

place: Harvard School of Public Health and Boston, Massachusetts
people: Philip Drinker (1894–1972), Harvard engineer
Louis A. Shaw, Harvard physiologist
Charles F. McKhann III, pediatrician
John Haven Emerson (1906–1997), maker of a cheaper rival machine
summary: A sealed metal tank that breathed for paralyzed patients set off a patent fight that turned on an 1864 precedent.
body: In 1929 Philip Drinker and Louis Shaw of the Harvard School of Public Health published the design of a negative-pressure respirator, a sealed tank enclosing the body, for keeping patients breathing over long periods. That year Drinker and the pediatrician Charles McKhann reported using it on a young polio patient. A Drinker machine cost around $3,600. John Haven Emerson built a quieter, simpler and cheaper one; when Drinker sued, his patents were declared invalid because body-enclosing respirators dated back to 1864.

links.note: Vaccines finally emptied the iron-lung wards.
Respirator wards for polio patients were a forerunner of intensive care.

title: Forssmann catheterizes his own heart

confidence.note: Forssmann published the self-experiment in 1929 with an X-ray image, and the Nobel Foundation's account confirms it. Retellings disagree on details such as the type of tube and whether the nurse helped him or was restrained.

place: August Victoria Home, Eberswalde, near Berlin
people: Werner Forssmann (1904–1979), surgical trainee
André Cournand and Dickinson Richards, New York physicians who developed the method
summary: A young German doctor pushed a tube up his own arm vein into his heart, then walked to X-ray to prove it. Recognition took 27 years.
body: In 1929, as a surgical trainee at Eberswalde near Berlin, Werner Forssmann passed a catheter 65 cm up a vein in his own arm, then walked to the X-ray department and photographed its tip in his heart's right atrium. He suggested such catheters could measure pressures and deliver contrast dye. His work was only moderately appreciated by colleagues and he went on to train in urology, while André Cournand and Dickinson Richards in New York made catheterization a clinical tool; all three shared the 1956 Nobel Prize.

myth.tradition: Forssmann strapped the nurse who was supposed to help him to the table, then catheterized himself.
myth.record: Published accounts disagree: some say he restrained the nurse, others that she cooperated. Only the self-experiment itself and the X-ray are well documented.

links.note: Catheter diagnosis helped make open-heart surgery possible.
Another way into the living heart, by its electricity rather than its chambers.
